title_original: Can Ali G: Who Iz I? save character comedy cinema?
editorial_title_zh: Can Ali G: Who Iz I? save character comedy cinema?
editorial_excerpt_zh: Sacha Baron Cohen’s new film risks being outdated in a more rancorous era. But could it restore the personality-driven genre to big screens or end it altogether? For a man whose campaign slogan was once “Keep it real”, Ali G has his work cut out in the reality of 2026. The big…

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "F or a man whose campaign slogan was once “Keep it real”, Ali G has his work cut out in the reality of 2026. The big dog of Da West Staines Massiv was the character with whom Sacha Baron Cohen carved out his own niche of gonzo-gotcha comedy in the late 1990s – and now he’s back with new film, Ali G: Who Iz I? But it’s unclear if his great creation has gone sufficiently fallow in the collective consciousness to still operate well in real-life situations, the kind of lethal idiot who once pitched Donald Trump anti-drip ice-cream gloves. And more critically, is the Ali G satirical project – which poked at 90s multicultural mores – still relevant and funny in far more rancorous times?", "links": [{"text": "Sacha Baron Cohen", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/culture/sacha-baron-cohen"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It’s not just Baron Cohen’s career as an undercover operative that’s on the line. It’s the future of character-led comedy as a going concern, now that he seems to be the last man standing in this once-noble tradition – in cinemas, at least. To be clear, character comedy isn’t merely comedy with characters; it’s comedy filtered through a central persona that overlaps with the comedian playing it and whose subversive sensibility colours the entire work."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/fd98d6ea50d262f3eb5839e0a8c30c8ade2030d4/0_42_1482_2077/master/1482.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Mike Myers’ swinging London exile … Myers and Heather Graham in Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me, 1999.", "caption": "Mike Myers’ swinging London exile … Myers and Heather Graham in Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me, 1999. Photograph: AJ Pics/Alamy", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mike Myers’ swinging London exile Austin Powers was the most commercially successful example – but the actor hasn’t made a film in that first-person style since his self-help spoof The Love Guru tanked in 2008. Will Ferrell , ruling the roost as fashion’s Dr Evil, Mugatu (in Zoolander), Buddy the Elf and Ron Burgundy, seemed the best successor. Mystifyingly, though, Ferrell has barely been able to get a film bankrolled in the last decade – and certainly not one putting him out front to that extent. Character comedy subsists on TV, from where it came, with the likes of Alan Partridge and Philomena Cunk. But unless the new Ali G can blaze a fresh hit of chronic satire into the genre’s bloodstream, it’s hard to see a future for it on the big screen.", "links": [{"text": "Will Ferrell", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/willferrell"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ali G was already controversial back in the day: the regular accusation was that while he was satirising the white appropriation of black culture, he in fact enabled straight lampooning of the latter. Now those criticisms are sharpened by the notion that, in 2026, he is past his sell-by date: both out of step with a more culturally mixed Britain and, overflowing with bifter gags and mad patois, dangerously adjacent to racist caricature that won’t pass these days. British standup comedian Dane Baptiste recently told Deadline : “After Black Lives Matter and the brief humanisation of black people and black creatives, it seems very dubious that we are now regressing back, not just five years, but 25 years, to bring back a character that was able to flourish because there were no accurate portrayals of black Britishness on screen.”", "links": [{"text": "recently told Deadline", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/09/ali-g-who-iz-i-writer-defends-amazon-sacha-baron-cohen-1237111031/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But it would be a shock if Baron Cohen wasn’t wise to the current sensitivities. In 2020’s Borat Subsequent Moviefilm , he mostly successfully updated the Kazakhstan reporter for the post-truth, Covid-era end times of Trump’s US. His choice of target interviewees in Who Iz I? remains to be seen, but it would be surprising if he didn’t pick a few where he can opportunistically needle both woke and anti-woke camps.", "links": [{"text": "Borat Subsequent Moviefilm", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2020/oct/21/borat-subsequent-moviefilm-review-sacha-baron-cohen-trump"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These debates are tricky ones, on cultural shifting sands, and Baron Cohen undeniably skirts close to reactionary goading at times (the fact that dumb Americans might actually believe Kazakhstan is that backward doesn’t escape the fact he’s propagating the idea it’s a potassium-, incest- and antisemitism-crazed shithole). But if the new Ali G film does fall foul of the post-Black Lives Matter climate, it’ll be hard not to also conclude that our splintered, fractious era lacks the unity – or at least consensus – that makes character comedy possible at all. To a large extent, audiences have to agree on the social phenomena these big satirical beasts feed off. article_text:
F or a man whose campaign slogan was once “Keep it real”, Ali G has his work cut out in the reality of 2026. The big dog of Da West Staines Massiv was the character with whom Sacha Baron Cohen carved out his own niche of gonzo-gotcha comedy in the late 1990s – and now he’s back with new film, Ali G: Who Iz I? But it’s unclear if his great creation has gone sufficiently fallow in the collective consciousness to still operate well in real-life situations, the kind of lethal idiot who once pitched Donald Trump anti-drip ice-cream gloves. And more critically, is the Ali G satirical project – which poked at 90s multicultural mores – still relevant and funny in far more rancorous times?

It’s not just Baron Cohen’s career as an undercover operative that’s on the line. It’s the future of character-led comedy as a going concern, now that he seems to be the last man standing in this once-noble tradition – in cinemas, at least. To be clear, character comedy isn’t merely comedy with characters; it’s comedy filtered through a central persona that overlaps with the comedian playing it and whose subversive sensibility colours the entire work.

Mike Myers’ swinging London exile Austin Powers was the most commercially successful example – but the actor hasn’t made a film in that first-person style since his self-help spoof The Love Guru tanked in 2008. Will Ferrell , ruling the roost as fashion’s Dr Evil, Mugatu (in Zoolander), Buddy the Elf and Ron Burgundy, seemed the best successor. Mystifyingly, though, Ferrell has barely been able to get a film bankrolled in the last decade – and certainly not one putting him out front to that extent. Character comedy subsists on TV, from where it came, with the likes of Alan Partridge and Philomena Cunk. But unless the new Ali G can blaze a fresh hit of chronic satire into the genre’s bloodstream, it’s hard to see a future for it on the big screen.

Ali G was already controversial back in the day: the regular accusation was that while he was satirising the white appropriation of black culture, he in fact enabled straight lampooning of the latter. Now those criticisms are sharpened by the notion that, in 2026, he is past his sell-by date: both out of step with a more culturally mixed Britain and, overflowing with bifter gags and mad patois, dangerously adjacent to racist caricature that won’t pass these days. British standup comedian Dane Baptiste recently told Deadline : “After Black Lives Matter and the brief humanisation of black people and black creatives, it seems very dubious that we are now regressing back, not just five years, but 25 years, to bring back a character that was able to flourish because there were no accurate portrayals of black Britishness on screen.”

But it would be a shock if Baron Cohen wasn’t wise to the current sensitivities. In 2020’s Borat Subsequent Moviefilm , he mostly successfully updated the Kazakhstan reporter for the post-truth, Covid-era end times of Trump’s US. His choice of target interviewees in Who Iz I? remains to be seen, but it would be surprising if he didn’t pick a few where he can opportunistically needle both woke and anti-woke camps.

These debates are tricky ones, on cultural shifting sands, and Baron Cohen undeniably skirts close to reactionary goading at times (the fact that dumb Americans might actually believe Kazakhstan is that backward doesn’t escape the fact he’s propagating the idea it’s a potassium-, incest- and antisemitism-crazed shithole). But if the new Ali G film does fall foul of the post-Black Lives Matter climate, it’ll be hard not to also conclude that our splintered, fractious era lacks the unity – or at least consensus – that makes character comedy possible at all. To a large extent, audiences have to agree on the social phenomena these big satirical beasts feed off. In the late 90s, black street culture was sufficiently new and prominent a force in the UK mainstream to make this crip-sign-throwing buffoon a direct hit.

There’s no reason why character comedy can’t thrive off societal shifts, though – if the character is positioned carefully enough. In fact, this is how it originally manufactured tension, with the likes of Charlie Chaplin’s Tramp getting fed through the mangler of industrialised capitalism in Modern Times. Or Peter Sellers playing both old establishment nabob Sir John Kennaway and the trade union firebrand Fred Kite in 1959’s labour-relations satire I’m All Right Jack. With postwar Britain evolving rapidly, Tony Hancock picked up the baton in 1961’s The Rebel, both surfing and sending up boho nonconformism in his role as an accidentally successful avant garde artist. Alan Partridge’s long slide into local radio-bound insignificance has only attained glorious new parallels in the post-Brexit era.

Another reason why character comedy may have fallen from favour is its vaudevillian strut, a very human theatricality that seems old-fashioned in an age of frictionless CGI blockbusters. It revels in transformation and disguise (Baron Cohen now, of course, being so famous he has to layer on disguises on top of his original disguises – hence the new Rasta Ali G). The genre often compounds this ludic chaos by having its stars play multiple roles, as Sellers, Eddie Murphy and Mike Myers love to do.

Somehow this protean fun allows the presiding comic genius’s essential quality to pierce through all the more clearly: in Sellers’ case, a kind of unnerving mildness that could transmute into mania, or Myers’ cheeky puerility. Mrs Doubtfire, from 1993, is one of the most revelatory uses of this ventriloquist effect. Another persona that the film’s divorced voiceover artist adopts in order to see his children more often, the Scottish nanny is really a conduit for the sentimental streak that underpinned much of Robin Williams’s work. And like the theatre, you can see the tactile human continuity between character comedy’s practitioners: Myers has often talked about his admiration for Sellers’ chameleonic powers. Dr Evil’s “one million dollars” faux pas is a lift of a similar gag near the end of Sellers’ 1959 geopolitics satire The Mouse That Roared.

By 2002, when Myers was doing silhouette gags about giving birth to Mini-Me in Austin Powers: Goldmember, this vaudevillian style was looking passe. With The Lord of the Rings and Harry Potter in full pomp, blockbuster film was firmly in the CGI era; comedy had moved on, too, to the edgier Frat Pack films and the realism of Judd Apatow.

But perhaps character comedy had also lost strong moorings by this point, with social comment largely absent from the genre since the 1980s. Instead, Austin Powers was an extended riff on 60s and 90s pop-cultural overlaps and discrepancies (Jean Dujardin did something similar in his later OSS-117 series), while Eddie Murphy’s multi-character outings The Nutty Professor and Norbit seemed largely there to prop up the fat-suit industry. Only Will Ferrell – via his blowhard news anchor Burgundy, but also in his general screen persona in ensemble work such as Wedding Crashers, Step Brothers and Talladega Nights – embodied a type that spoke clearly for the times: the arrested manchild.

That all changed the moment Borat and his wobbling producer Azamat Bagatov landed in New York in 2006. By injecting Borat with a raw hit of the reality format incubated on The 11 O’Clock Show and Da Ali G Show, Baron Cohen completely revitalised big-screen character comedy. Suddenly, it became thrillingly politicised as his sublimely ignorant aliases, Borat and in 2009 Brüno, flushed out American and Middle Eastern absurdities and prejudices. Not to mention the high-wire aspect of his escapades: Baron Cohen was somehow impervious to whatever peril he stirred up, whether that was desecrating the Star-Spangled Banner at a rodeo in Borat, or an interpretation of mano-a-mano quite different to what cage fighting audiences were expecting in Brüno. His gleeful brazenness was the signature quality that shone through.

But Ali G has been dormant a long time. His last big-screen outing, 2002’s hit-and-miss Ali G Indahouse , was a very different, fully scripted endeavour. Beyond a gag about mistaking a pregnancy test for a vape, the trailer for Ali G: Who Iz I? doesn’t give much away about how sharply the character’s been updated; judging by the small-penis outro, some things are undying.

Staines’s favourite son will need to pull more out of his XXXXXL puffa. Only the current culture wars – police violence, colonialism, cultural appropriation – can supply him with appropriately charged material that he can “booyakasha” his way through. Anything less, and the character’s age will show, and the once-cutting posturing and patois will seem less than ironic. Which would be a bad thing for character comedy – then the mask really will have slipped.

For the last two weeks, we’ve handed over The Film Comment Podcast to the participants of the 2026 Film at Lincoln Center Critics Academy —an annual program for up-and-coming critics held during the New York Film Festival, led by Film Comment editors.

On this week’s episode , four of this year’s critics—Eliel Peterson, Brennan Ryan, Auhjanae McGee, and Brian O’Connell—discuss some of their highlights from NYFF’s Spotlight Shorts and New York Shorts programs, including Kamal Aljafari’s Masao Adachi Takes a Passport Photo , Camilo Restrepo’s A Stolen Movie , and Heather Landsman’s ee .

article_text:
Japan’s entertainment business has to adopt the model that made Hollywood studios global players if the country wants to reach its content export targets, according to Shiina Yasushi , CEO of TIFFCOM , the Tokyo International Film Festival ‘s content market now heading into its 23rd edition.

The Japanese government has set a target of JPY20 trillion ($126.6 billion) in overseas content sales by 2033, and expects anime to bring in JPY6 trillion ($38 billion) of that. Shiina argues that looking abroad won’t be enough without a change in how Japanese companies operate.

“Historically, Japanese companies have often licensed content rights abroad and left local distribution and marketing to their licensees. Going forward, companies should retain ownership of their IP, be actively involved in international distribution, and maximize the revenue generated from their properties,” Shiina tells Variety .

He points out that Hollywood studios reached global scale by setting up their own distribution operations country by country and dealing with each market directly. Japan should take the same route, he says. With that base in place, a property can then be spread across film, games, streaming and merchandise. Shiina sees this as the shift to the “IP-driven industry” the government has called for.

Japanese companies have begun rethinking how they handle IP. TBS is working with Legendary Entertainment, Nippon TV is expanding internationally and publishers are looking at overseas adaptations. Shiina says a fundamental shift is under way. “In the past, the very concept of the long-term value of IP was not widely considered,” he says. Talent agencies have also started paying attention to IP, he adds, because the IP a performer worked on can live on long after they retire.

According to Shiina, the market itself has changed most in who attends. TIFFCOM used to be mainly a place where international sales agents traded finished content. Once producers arrived, it became a more creative market. Streamers now attend next to film and TV companies, and the IP holders on the floor include anime studios, publishers, game companies and toy makers.

The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market (TGFM) is now big enough to build programs around specific regions and genres, Shiina says. Alongside its Asian focus, it has a collaboration with Italy and, this year, a partnership with Canada’s genre outfit Frontières. When TGFM started, it simply picked projects that met its eligibility rules.

The aim is to make Tokyo a key stop for developing and financing projects, as well as for selling finished ones. “While traditional markets centered on sellers and buyers, our vision is a marketplace where everyone involved in production comes together – from producers, directors, and screenwriters to studios and investors providing capital,” Shiina says.

Taking the Tokyo IP Market to the Cannes Film Market raised TIFFCOM’s profile. Even so, Shiina says the goal isn’t simply to repeat that move at other overseas markets. The priority is still getting international professionals to come to Japan.

“Japan possesses such compelling IP that creators and producers around the world want to collaborate with us. By coming to Japan, international partners can engage in direct, face-to-face dialogue with creators – including original authors, directors, and screenwriters,” he says.

At Cannes, Japan was Country of Honor. Its delegation included sales executives, directors, producers, studios and senior company leaders. Because the program featured anime studios and IP as well as live-action, publishers went too. For Shiina, the biggest result was a change in attitude. Japanese executives who used to see festival markets only as places to buy and sell finished films found out they could take part themselves.

He wants to keep that from being a one-time event. “If Cannes was the first step, this edition of Tokyo represents the second step, and we are still just at the beginning. By sustaining this virtuous cycle, we aim to build a lasting, sustainable business,” Shiina says.

TIFFCOM’s technology keynote this year features AGBO executives speaking about AI and storytelling. Shiina won’t predict which part of the business AI will change first. He is sure, though, that it will reshape production by lowering costs and shortening turnaround. Rights are his main worry, and he says the whole industry needs to work on frameworks for them.

“The critical priority is how to protect creators. This year’s keynote features AGBO – a studio founded by film directors – speaking on how to leverage AI and technology in a creator-led manner, which I believe is precisely the topic the industry wants to hear right now,” he says.

Shiina doesn’t think Japan can settle the AI question alone. Both the technology and the rights involved cross borders, and he says opting out of AI is no longer realistic.

On anime’s long-running problems with costs, working conditions and creators’ share of profits, Shiina says things are getting better, though slowly. He cites work-style reforms, a new law protecting freelancers, and joint government and industry efforts on working conditions. Studios are also starting to keep their IP and build their own businesses instead of working only as subcontractors, and live-action producers are doing the same. “I believe anime is leading the way worldwide, with live-action following in its footsteps,” he says.

Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market and Hong Kong FilMart are also chasing international growth. Shiina says a market should be judged on quality, not numbers. “When industry professionals plan their annual calendars, Tokyo remains an unmissable destination because it allows them to connect directly with Japanese rights holders and creators,” he says. Getting more Japanese companies to take part is the key, he adds, because international attendance follows Japanese participation.

Looking ahead, Shiina wants to expand TIFFCOM’s capacity across its whole operation, not just its floor space. “By around 2030, including venue expansion, we envision growing TIFFCOM into a significantly expanded marketplace,” he says.

title_original: 「JUMP アーティスト＋キュレーター国際協働プログラム」、海外3都市での展示概要を発表
editorial_title_zh: “JUMP艺术家+策展人国际协作项目”公布在海外3座城市举办的展览概要
editorial_excerpt_zh: 10月15日，国立艺术研究中心（NCAR）公布了培养项目“JUMP”在海外3座城市的展览概要。由远藤薰与荒井保洋（悉尼）、青柳菜摘与见留沙耶香（里斯本）、MES与冢本麻莉（洛杉矶）这3组共计7人带来的成果展将于2026年11月起陆续举办。 The post 「JUMP アーティスト＋キュレーター国際協働プログラム」、海外3都市での展示概要を発表 first appeared on ART iT（アートイット） .

article_text:
2026年10月15日、国立アートリサーチセンター（NCAR）は、日本の若手アーティストとキュレーターの国際的な活躍を目的とする育成プログラム「JUMP アーティスト＋キュレーター国際協働プログラム」の海外3都市（シドニー、リスボン、ロサンゼルス）での展示概要を発表した。 日本のアーティストとキュレーター3組計7名 が、現地の美術館と約1年半にわたり協働してきたプロジェクトの成果展示を、2026年11月より順次開催する。 JUMPは、日本の新進アーティストと若手キュレーターの国際的な活躍を支援する育成プログラムとして2024年度にスタートした。海外3都市の美術館の協力のもと、3組のアーティストとキュレーターが、複数回にわたる海外滞在を通じてリサーチを行ない、それに基づく作品を制作し、現地の美術館で展示を行なう。育成対象となるキュレーターは公募で選出され、国際経験や語学力などは不問としながらも、選出後は海外美術館との協働を通じて国際的な経験やネットワークを広げながら、各地でのリサーチに基づく企画・作品制作に取り組んできた。2026年7月には 「Open Talk Meet Up!」 と題して、これまでのリサーチの様子や海外美術館との協働、展示のコンセプトなどの報告会を行なった。

2026年11月7日（土）より、ニュー・サウス・ウェールズ州立美術館（オーストラリア・シドニー）のアジアランタンギャラリーにおいて、アーティストの 遠藤薫 （1989年大阪府生まれ）と滋賀県立美術館主任学芸員の 荒井保洋 （1986年福岡県生まれ）による展示「Sleeping in the 22nd Century（二十二世紀の睡眠法）」が開幕する。本展に向けて、遠藤と荒井は2026年4月にシドニー市内各所をめぐったほか、オーストラリア北部・ダーウィンを訪問し、アボリジナルの人々の語りに登場する「ライトニングマン」や「レインボーサーペント」についてリサーチした。ニュー・サウス・ウェールズ州立美術館には、アボリジナルの人々が受け継いできた文化に対して盗用を防ぐための厳しいルールがあり、先住民文化との関わり方については、アボリジナルのキュレーターと協議しながら進められた。遠藤は当初、 国際芸術祭「あいち2022」 で発表した《羊と眠る》のような、羊をモチーフとした展覧会を構想していたが、オーストラリアの厳しい検疫体制や、同館の規則上、有機物の使用が難しいことから、同作の背景にもあった夢を軸とする展示へと変更した。本展は、オーストラリア滞在中に経験した一連の予知夢に応答して制作されたサイトスペシフィックなインスタレーションで、和紙に描いた水墨画、テキスタイル、映像を組み合わせ、それぞれが蛇、水、虹にまつわる古代の神話や図像、龍神の伝説や古代日本の文字に基づいている。会場には遠藤の夢日記が随所に現れ、遠藤はその意味を解釈するために人工知能を用いる。そこではAIが無意識の延長として機能し、直観、記憶、想像力が媒介され、変容していく。

11月28日（土）からは、CAM – グルベンキアン・モダンアートセンター（ポルトガル・リスボン）のサウンドルームとスタジオにて、アーティストの 青柳菜摘 （1990年東京都生まれ）と山口情報芸術センター［YCAM］キュレーターの 見留さやか （1986年生まれ）による展示「Sanitary Fables（衛生寓話）」が続く。青柳が初めてポルトガルを訪れた際に行なったフィールドワークで、歴史的な貯水池との出会いと古い洗濯場の静けさが公衆衛生への関心をかき立て、本展の構想につながった。2026年4月にCAMのディレクターが代わり、サブ会場として使用するはずだった小さな展示室しか使えなくなったことから、ふたりは6月末にリスボンに滞在して展示プランを練り直し、洗濯場や書店、アートスペースなどでリスボンのまちの人々と交流を重ねた。本展は、リスボンの下水道と公衆衛生のインフラを調査し、都市を流れるその流路をたどるビデオ・インスタレーションとなる。青柳は、きれいと汚いを分ける衛生という概念は社会に分断を生み出してしまうかもしれないとし、「衛生」がつくってしまった分断を「寓話」という形式で崩すことを試みる。ここで「衛生」は自らの生命を守る行為として理解され、本作は寓話と人間ならざるものの視点を通した現代社会の再発見を提案する。作品は美術館内にとどまらず、公共洗濯場を含むリスボン市内のさまざまな場所にまたがり、来場者は地図を手にリスボンを探索しながら、作品がその経路に織り込む寓話を見つけていく。

さらに2027年2月25日（木）からは、ロサンゼルス現代美術館（アメリカ・ロサンゼルス）のゲフェン・コンテンポラリーで、アーティストデュオ、 MES の 新井健 （1991年千葉県生まれ）、 谷川果菜絵 （1991年北海道生まれ）と高知県立美術館主任学芸員の 塚本麻莉 （1989年大阪府生まれ）による展示「セイ/SE-I/SAY」が開催される。2025年のリサーチでは、第二次世界大戦中に日系アメリカ人が収容されたマンザナー強制収容所を訪問し、2026年2月の1カ月間の滞在では、ロサンゼルスにある日系アメリカ人博物館で行なわれた日系人の「追憶の日」のセレモニーに参加した。こうしたリサーチを重ね、MESと塚本は、高知にもゆかりのあるジャーナリストで、大逆事件によって処刑された幸徳秋水をモチーフにしたパフォーマンス形式のインスタレーションを展示・上演する。幸徳は1905年に渡米し、現地のアナキストらと交流した人物で、大逆事件の判決に対してはアメリカ合衆国でも抗議運動が起こった。本作は、20世紀初頭の日米のアナキストたちによる、国境を越えた連帯の歴史を参照する新作で、幸徳らの言葉、MES自身の声、身体の熱を映し出すサーモグラフィー映像、紙吹雪が舞う祝祭的な演出を通じて、連帯と抵抗の歴史を現代に呼び起こす。会期中の木曜から日曜の午後の時間帯で連続した4時間もの間、MESのふたりが展示会場でパフォーマンスを通しで行なう。 メンターを務める国立アートリサーチセンターエグゼクティブアドバイザー、森美術館館長の片岡真実は、「長く続くネットワークを構築するためには、共に仕事を成し遂げ、信頼に基づいた人間関係を結ぶことがいちばん」と考え、国際協働を実感する仕組みとしてJUMPをデザインしたと述べ、「この機会に国境も言語の壁も、そして未知の世界への躊躇など、さまざまな境界線を飛び越え、その先に長く続く関係性を育てていただけることを期待しています」とコメントしている。制作プロセスは JUMPウェブサイト で公開されており、海外での展示終了後は、国内3カ所（山口、高知、滋賀）でも作品の展示を予定している。

article_text:
Tom Hanks will star in the play “This World of Tomorrow,” marking his return to Broadway for the first time in 14 years.

Hanks was last on Broadway in Nora Ephron’s 2013 play “Lucky Guy,” which earned him a Tony nomination. This time, the celebrated actor will be joined by theater veteran Kelli O’Hara, who appeared alongside him in the show’s Off Broadway run last year at the Shed.

“This World of Tomorrow” is based on a series of short stories written by Hanks. He’s co-writing the adaptation with James Glossman. Described as a “time-travel romance,” the play takes place at the end of the 21st century and follows Bert Allenberry, who is determined to change his future by returning to the past. “When Bert journeys back — again, and again, and again — to one remarkable day at the 1939 New York World’s Fair in Queens, he discovers that the future is shaped not by technology, but by the choices we make for love,” per the official logline.

Related Stories

'Harry Potter' HBO Series Casts Sorting Hat, Nearly Headless Nick, and More Hogwarts Ghosts and Portraits

J.K. Rowling’s Agent Slams Trans Rights Protest at ‘Harry Potter and the Cursed Child’ in London: It Put ‘Others at Risk’

Directed by Kenny Leon, whose recent Broadway credits include “The Balusters,” “Othello” with Denzel Washington and Jake Gyllenhaal, and “Our Town” with Jim Parsons and Katie Holmes, is directing the show. It will play at a Shubert theater to be announced. Complete cast and creative team details will be confirmed soon.

“I’m so excited to continue this work on this amazing new American play,” said Leon. “There’s no time like the present to further explore this story of love and time travel from Glossman and Hanks. More than anything, I look forward to even more audiences who will have the chance to witness the onstage chemistry of Kelli O’Hara and Tom Hanks.”

Adds The Shed’s artistic director Alex Poots, “A beloved actor of our times, Tom Hanks co-created and starred in ‘This World of Tomorrow’ with the illuminating Kelli O’Hara for their sold out run at The Shed. Reminding us that while the world changes, the deepest of human connections endures and the power of love can transcend any era. Now this story of second chances gets to reach an even wider audience on Broadway.”

Producer Brian Anthony Moreland described Hanks as “one of the great storytellers of our time” and called it an “incredible privilege” to bring this play to Broadway.

“There is something extraordinary about bringing a story that explores the power of love across time to a place where the magic of live theater happens every night,” Moreland said. “At its heart, ‘This World of Tomorrow’ reminds us that no matter how much the world changes, the one thing that remains timeless is our capacity to love.”

editorial_title_zh: 为什么所有人都讨厌伦敦的90年代展？
editorial_excerpt_zh: 为什么所有人都讨厌伦敦的90年代展？ Saskia Trebing Wed, 10/28/2026 - 15:00
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "爱德华·恩宁福（Edward Enninful）对90年代英国艺术与时尚的纵览被批为流于表面且混乱不堪。然而，如此动荡的一个十年本来就无法以井然有序的结构来展示", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "英国艺术界的抗议声是不是太猛烈了？在参观泰特不列颠美术馆（Tate Britain）弗里兹周特展“90年代：艺术与时尚”（The 90s: Art and Fashion）时，这个问题让人挥之不去。自10月6日以一场热闹非凡的私人派对开幕以来，这场试图将一个十年的英国文化浓缩于一场清晰、精炼展览中的尝试遭遇了严厉的批评。当然，《每日电讯报》（The Telegraph）和《独立报》（The Independent）给出了五星好评，但这些赞美之词淹没在一片更喧嚣、更愤世嫉俗的批评合唱之中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在朋友圈子里，这种共识甚至更加毫不留情。在填满弗里兹日程表的众多开幕式和派对上，伦敦那些骄傲自负、极具意见领袖气质的文化鉴赏家们似乎终于达成了一致：“90年代”是一个浅薄、策展混乱的大杂烩。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "跳出英国本土的圈子来看，这种鄙视令人惊讶，部分原因在于策展人正是那个时代的标志性人物：爱德华·恩宁福（在泰特美术馆五位策展团队成员的协助下）。在担任英国版《Vogue》主编的几十年前，恩宁福几乎在整个90年代都在《i-D》杂志担任时装总监——他在1991年以刚满18岁的年纪接任了这一职务。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对一切逝去事物的回忆", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种根基被视作优势而非劣势：恩宁福的名字出现在宣传海报上。他在1991年由杰森·埃文斯（Jason Evans）为《i-D》拍摄的名为《Strictly》的照片甚至挂在展览中。然而，正是在参观展览的过程中，这种内部人士的身份愈发让人觉得这才是真正的问题所在。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正如对过去的每一次致敬一样，展览似乎透过那些曾亲历该十年之人的玫瑰色眼镜来审视它——恩宁福也不例外。然而，对于在英国脱欧后长大成人的一代人来说，“酷不列颠”（Cool Britannia）的自信或许更像是一曲对所有逝去事物的回忆，而非对那个十年文化成就的赞颂。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://monopol-prod.nbg1.your-objectstorage.com/s3fs-public/styles/max1560x1150/public/2026-10/The%2090s%20Art%20and%20Fashion%20at%20Tate%20Britain.%20Photo%20%C2%A9%20Tate%20%28Lucy%20Green%29%20%281%29.jpeg?itok=bXRMf8XD", "alt": "Großes Foto zentral, kleinere Arbeiten; rechts Tapete mit Augen; Besucher:in in Ausstellungsraum.", "caption": "Photo © Tate (Lucy Green) \"The 90s: Art and Fashion,\" Tate Britain", "credit": "Monopol", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "由于在进展之前就带着如此多的成见，我感觉自己仿佛生来就被设定好要痛批它。当我步入七个展厅中的第一个时，这种印象也并未减轻。英国年轻艺术家（YBA）萨拉·卢卡斯（Sarah Lucas）的作品《1-123-123-12-12》（1991）——一双鞋头塞满剃须刀片的马丁靴（Dr. Martens）——正放在正中央的一堆灰色水泥砖上。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "墙上挂着那些曾经无处不在、以至于其曾经革命性的光芒已经褪色、如今显得理所当然且老生常谈的图像：沃尔夫冈·蒂尔曼斯（Wolfgang Tillmans）经常被重印的《苏珊与鲁茨，白裙，军装裙》（Suzanne & Lutz, white dress, army skirt，1993），尤尔根·特勒（Jürgen Teller）的一小批照片；芭芭拉·沃克（Barbara Walker）的画作《态度》（Attitude，1998），以及科琳·戴（Corinne Day）拍摄的凯特·摩丝（Kate Moss）照片，这张照片在1993年英国版《Vogue》的一篇报道中用圣诞彩灯装裱起来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "由于我的视线已被确认偏误所模糊，这些“精选大作”似乎证明了关于这是一场简单且无聊展览的传言确凿无疑。但随后，我注意到一件奇怪的绿色吊带裙，它悬浮在通往下一个展厅入口处的喧嚣上方不远处。当我走近时，墙上的文字告诉我，这件看似普通的裙子竟然出自斯特拉·麦卡特尼（Stella McCartney）之手——她正是90年代最著名的“靠父辈余荫走红的星二代”（Nepo-Baby）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "设计师的基因优势？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这种语境下，它被抬高的位置仿佛成了一个恰如其分（且可能完全无意）的视觉玩笑，讽刺了这位设计师天生自带的优越起点。或者，它被挂在那里纯粹只是为了在拥挤的空间里节省地方？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这件麦卡特尼的遗物将人引向了一个带来情绪冲击的展厅。这里到处都是身体、身体、还是身体。有些身体，例如女画家珍妮·萨维尔（Jenny Saville）在与摄影师格伦·勒奇福德（Glen Luchford）合作拍摄《闭密接触 #4》（Closed Contact #4，1995–96）时被压在玻璃上。另一些则变成了覆盖整面墙的厚颜无耻的印花，比如阿比盖尔·莱恩（Abigail Lane）的《屁股壁纸》（Bottom Wallpaper，1994）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "整个展览有一种绝妙的古怪感。当然，有些作品确实让人忍不住翻白眼——例如萨拉·卢卡斯的《鸡肉内裤》（Chicken Knickers，1997）保质期大概也就和绑在模特胯部的生肉差不多——但那种纯粹的混乱能量冲淡了我进来时的消极态度。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "看到一把木椅子正对着一面贴满蓝色屁股印记的墙时，我意识到，与其说这是一场展览，不如说它更应该被当作一种迪士尼乐园式的景点来体验：“这是一个小小世界”（it’s a small world），只不过里面挤满了整个十年的遗物，而不是那些可疑的电子动画，并由一种不屑于除“90年代”之外任何叙事主线的发散性策展方法所主导。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "所有他们警告过我的事情，既是真实的，又是虚假的。“The 90s”在某些地方无疑是肤浅的，它罗列了该年代艺术和时尚界最大牌的杰作。但它也深入探讨了文化的更偏门利基——其中重点呈现了黑人设计师、摄影师和艺术家的贡献。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "令人眩晕的旅程", "translated": true}, "面对我们这个时代的复杂性与矛盾性，这场展览在抵制其自身的怀旧情绪时表现得最为出色。在一条仿佛存在于另一个世界的黑暗走廊尽头，我遇到了史蒂夫·麦奎因（Steve McQueen）具有开创性的无声电影《Bear》（1993）。整整30年后，这位艺术家与另一个男人的紧张、无言的对峙——两人赤身裸体，以高对比度的黑白胶片拍摄——依然比主导最后一个展厅的约翰·加利亚诺（John Galliano）或薇薇安·韦斯特伍德（Vivienne Westwood）的任何一件裙装，都更有效地抽干了房间里的空气。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在经历了这场对恩宁弗（Enninful）破碎而万花筒般的年代赞歌、令人眩晕的旅程之后，关于英国艺术界是否抗议过于严厉的问题似乎已经有了答案：是的，确实如此。这场展览过于拥挤、不够均衡而且往往过于显眼，但它的杂乱无章正契合了它所描绘的那个时代。你不必亲历那个年代也能享受这段旅程。你只需要把你的犬儒主义留在门外。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Edward Enninfuls Überblick über britische Kunst und Mode der 90er-Jahre wurde als oberflächlich und chaotisch verrissen. Doch ein so unstetes Jahrzehnt kann gar nicht ordentlich strukturiert ausgestellt werden

Protestiert die britische Kunstwelt zu heftig? Diese Frage ließ sich bei einem Besuch der Frieze-Week-Schau "The 90s: Art and Fashion" in der Tate Britain unmöglich verdrängen. Seit der Eröffnung mit einer gut besuchten Privatparty am 6. Oktober hat der Versuch, ein Jahrzehnt britischer Kultur in einer klaren, prägnanten Ausstellung zusammenzufassen, harsche Kritik einstecken müssen. Sicher, "The Telegraph" und "The Independent" vergaben glänzende Fünf-Sterne-Kritiken, doch diese Lobeshymnen gingen in einem lauteren, zynischeren Chor der Verrisse unter.

Innerhalb von Freundeskreisen war der Konsens sogar noch unerbittlicher. Bei den zahlreichen Vernissagen und Partys, die den Frieze-Kalender füllten, schienen sich Londons stolz-snobistische, aggressiv meinungsstarke Kulturkenner endlich einmal einig zu sein: "The 90s" sei ein seichtes, chaotisch kuratiertes Durcheinander.

Von außerhalb der britischen Blase betrachtet war diese Verachtung überraschend, zum Teil weil die Kuration von einer Schlüsselfigur jener Ära verantwortet wurde: Edward Enninful (mit Unterstützung von fünf Mitgliedern des kuratorischen Teams der Tate). Jahrzehnte, bevor er die britische "Vogue" leitete, verbrachte Enninful fast die gesamten 90er-Jahre als Modedirektor bei "i-D" – eine Position, die er 1991 im Alter von gerade einmal 18 Jahren übernahm.

Erinnerung an alles Verlorene

Diese Verankerung wird als Vorteil und nicht als Nachteil dargestellt: Enninfuls Name erscheint auf den Werbeplakaten. Ein Bild von ihm aus "Strictly", einem i-D-Shooting von Jason Evans aus dem Jahr 1991, hängt sogar in der Ausstellung. Doch genau dieser Insider-Status fühlte sich beim Besuch der Schau zunehmend wie das eigentliche Problem an.

Wie bei jeder Hommage an die Vergangenheit schien die Ausstellung das Jahrzehnt durch die rosarote Brille derer zu betrachten, die es selbst erlebt hatten – Enninful eingeschlossen. Doch für eine Generation, die im Vereinigten Königreich nach dem Brexit erwachsen wurde, mag die Selbstsicherheit von "Cool Britannia" eher wie eine Erinnerung an alles Verlorene gewirkt haben als wie eine Würdigung der kulturellen Errungenschaften dieses Jahrzehnts.

Da ich schon vor dem Betreten der Ausstellung so viel Vorurteile mitbrachte, hatte ich das Gefühl, darauf programmiert zu sein, sie zu verreißen. Dieser Eindruck ließ auch nicht nach, als ich den ersten der sieben Räume betrat. Das Werk "1-123-123-12-12" (1991) der Young-British-Artists-Künstlerin Sarah Lucas – ein Paar Dr. Martens, in deren Zehen Rasierklingen gestopft waren – stand auf einem Stapel grauer Zementziegel in der Mitte.

An den Wänden hingen Bilder, die so allgegenwärtig waren, dass ihr einst revolutionärer Glanz verblasst war und sie nun einfach nur noch selbstverständlich und abgedroschen wirkten: Wolfgang Tillmans’ oft nachgedrucktes "Suzanne & Lutz, white dress, army skirt“"(1993) und eine Handvoll kleiner Bilder von Jürgen Teller; Barbara Walkers Gemälde "Attitude" (1998) und Corinne Days Foto von Kate Moss, eingerahmt von Weihnachtslichtern für eine Reportage in der britischen "Vogue" von 1993.

Da meine Sicht bereits durch Bestätigungsfehler getrübt war, schienen diese "Greatest Hits" zu beweisen, dass das Gerede von einer einfachen, langweiligen Ausstellung der Wahrheit entsprach. Doch dann fiel mir ein merkwürdiges grünes Slipdress auf, das knapp über dem Trubel schwebte, über dem Eingang zum nächsten Raum. Als ich näher trat, verriet mir der Wandtext, dass dieses scheinbar gewöhnliche Kleid von niemand Geringerem als Stella McCartney entworfen worden war – dem berühmtesten "Nepo-Baby" der 90er-Jahre.

Genetischer Vorsprung einer Designerin?

In diesem Zusammenhang wirkte seine erhöhte Platzierung wie ein treffender (und vielleicht völlig unbeabsichtigter) visueller Witz über den genetisch bedingten Vorsprung der Designerin. Oder hatte man es vielleicht einfach nur dort aufgehängt, um in dem überfüllten Raum Platz zu sparen?

Dieses McCartney-Relikt führte in einen Raum, der einen stimmungsmäßigen Schock auslöste. Hier gab es Körper, Körper, Körper. Einige, wie die der Malerin Jenny Saville, waren im Rahmen ihrer Zusammenarbeit mit dem Fotografen Glen Luchford für "Closed Contact #4" (1995–96) gegen Glas gepresst worden. Andere waren zu einem frechen Druck geworden, der eine ganze Wand bedeckte, wie in Abigail Lanes "Bottom Wallpaper" (1994).

Das Ganze hatte etwas brillant Skurriles an sich. Sicher, manche Werke ließen einen die Augen verdrehen – Sarah Lucas’ "Chicken Knickers" (1997) zum Beispiel ist etwa so gut gealtert wie das rohe Fleisch, das am Schritt des Modells befestigt war –, aber die schiere chaotische Energie verdrängte die negative Einstellung, mit der ich hereingekommen war.

Beim Anblick eines Holzstuhls, der einer Wand aus blauen Hinternabdrücken zugewandt war, wurde mir klar, dass man dies weniger als Ausstellung, sondern eher als eine Art Disneyland-Attraktion erleben sollte: "it’s a small world", allerdings überfüllt mit Relikten eines ganzen Jahrzehnts statt fragwürdiger Animatronik und geleitet von einem umwälschenden Kurationsansatz, der an keiner narrativen Leitlinie jenseits von "den 90ern" interessiert zu sein scheint.

Mit dieser Einstellung war jeder weitere Raum ein Abenteuer oder ein Spukhaus. Eine überwältigende Ode an die Musik, geprägt von einer wandfüllenden Fotocollage staubiger Raves (und der Raver mit großen Pupillen, die daran teilnahmen), wich dem Schock der blutigen Verstümmelungs-Skulptur der Chapman-Brüder, "Great Deeds Against the Dead" (1994), in einem abgedunkelten Raum, der den Körpern gewidmet war – ja, schon wieder, doch diesmal ging es auch um Aids.

Dort stand Alexander McQueens auffälliges rotes, mit Glasperlen besetztes Kleid aus seiner feurigen Herbst/Winter-Show "Joan" von 1998 in Sichtweite der Formaldehyd-Haie von Damien Hirst, einem weiteren YBA-Wunderkind, die auf einem runden Metallrohr in einem gleißend weißen Raum thronten, der dem "Minimalismus" gewidmet war. (Na, verstanden?)

Alles, wovor man mich gewarnt hatte, war wahr und unwahr zugleich. "The 90s" war zweifellos stellenweise oberflächlich und zählte Werke der größten Namen des Jahrzehnts aus Kunst und Mode auf. Doch sie tauchte auch in obskurere Nischen der Kultur ein – wobei vor allem Beiträge von Schwarzen Designern, Fotografen und Künstlern im Mittelpunkt standen.

Schwindelerregende Reise

Die Kuration war ein chaotisches Durcheinander, aber das war das Jahrzehnt ja auch. Die 90er waren MTV und Madonna und McQueen, und sie waren auch der Zusammenbruch der Sowjetunion und das Aufkommen des "Heroin-Chic" (und von echtem Heroin).

Angesichts der Komplexität und der Widersprüche unserer Zeit war die Ausstellung dann am besten, wenn sie ihrer eigenen Nostalgie widerstand. Am Ende eines dunklen Korridors, der in einer anderen Welt zu existieren schien, stieß ich auf Steve McQueens bahnbrechenden Stummfilm "Bear" (1993). Gut 30 Jahre später raubte die spannungsgeladene, wortlose Konfrontation des Künstlers mit einem anderen Mann – beide nackt und in kontrastreichem Schwarz-Weiß gefilmt – dem Raum immer noch wirkungsvoller den Sauerstoff als jedes Kleid von John Galliano oder Vivienne Westwood, das den letzten Raum dominierte.

Nach dieser schwindelerregenden Reise durch Enninfuls zerbrochene, kaleidoskopische Ode an das Jahrzehnt schien die Frage, ob die britische Kunstwelt zu harsch protestiert, beantwortet: Ja, das tut sie. Die Ausstellung ist überladen, unausgewogen und oft zu offensichtlich, aber ihr Wirrwarr passt zu dem Jahrzehnt, das sie darstellt. Man muss es nicht selbst erlebt haben, um die Reise zu genießen. Man muss nur seinen Zynismus an der Tür abgeben.

article_text:
When Christopher Nolan gathered his team of artisans for his adaptation of Homer’s epic poem “ The Odyssey ” he first told production designer Ruth De Jong of his plans.

But the process was shrouded in secrecy because working with Nolan is an in-person process. De Jong explained, “There are no scripts emailed, sent or discussed on any form of device. Everything is in person, which I love about him.”

Related Stories

‘Decision to Leave’ Cinematographer Kim Ji-yong on Chasing Natural Light for Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’: ‘This Is the One Where We Worried, Debated and Planned the Most’

'Nobody Wants This' Season 3 Opens With 6.2 Million Views in Four Days

De Jong was speaking with Variety’s senior artisans editor Jazz Tangcay at the Middleburg Film Festival, where she was honored alongside costume designer Ellen Mirojnick and editor Jennifer Lame with Variety’s Creative Collaborators Award.

De Jong, who had worked with Nolan on “Oppenheimer,” read the script in three hours. When she was done, she asked about the parameters. “He said, ‘There aren’t.’” The world was her oyster.

“Working with Chris is the closest thing. It’s equivalent to playing basketball with Kobe Bryant. He’s truly the ultimate collaborator and coach.” She adds, “I knew we weren’t going to fail, but I had no idea how we were going to do this practically.”

From the fall of Troy to Circe’s isolated home to Odysseus’ boat, De Jong brought Nolan’s vision to life across six countries: Morocco, Greece, Italy, Iceland, Scotland and the United States, building practical sets along the way.

Mirojnick and Lame were brought onto the project the same way; Nolan invited them to his house to read the script. She said Nolan didn’t want a “sword-and-sandal movie. Not a Hollywood movie, not something we had seen before.”

Mirojnick and her team created over 5,300 total costumes for the film, but it was a giant undertaking. “The armor had to be done first,” she says and with that she had “to think of a thousand people in different armies, the Trojans and the Spartans.”

Next was figuring out Odysseus. Mirojnick said, “The one thing we understood from Ruth’s research was that there were two fabrics at that time, one of which was linen. Linen gives you a great ground to age, distress and make into anything that you want. It was quite interesting seeing sand, salt, wind, rain and black sand mixing that all together and how that affects the fabric.”

Lame is no stranger to editing Nolan’s famous non-linear timelines, such as “Tenet” and “Oppenheimer.” she cut 2.1 million feet of 70mm Imax film for “The Odyssey.”

The Polyphemus scene, in particular, proved to be a puzzle. Lame recalled, “There was so much interesting material to use and mine.”

In the scene, Odysseus and his men enter a cave filled with cheese and sheep, only to discover it is the home of Polyphemus, the son of Poseidon. Odysseus tricks the Cyclops by telling him his name is “Nobody.” When Polyphemus passes out, Odysseus and his men drive a wooden stake into his single eye. As they make their escape, Odysseus foolishly taunts the Cyclops and reveals his real name. Polyphemus prays to his father Poseidon to curse Odysseus, dooming him on a long and perilous journey.

De Jong revealed that, from the beginning, Nolan wanted the Cyclops to be physically present in the cave. “We scoured a lot of places with some really cool, interesting caves, all of which we critiqued heavily. We scouted this area in Greece, and we were scouting these palace ruins. The cave was underneath us, but it was 100 degrees in Greece in September and we just kept going on our scout.”

At one point, they considered building the cave, but De Jong admitted, “It felt like using the resources to construct a cave — they’re expensive. And I was like, ‘Surely we can do this practically.’” Eventually, they found the perfect spot. The location allowed the boats to be placed practically at the bottom of the mountain, which helped everyone connect the dots.

The scene was practically shot with Bill Irwin playing the Cyclops. Lame explained, “We were all working together. Visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson and his team would do this crazy temp eye work, so we could always see what Bill’s eye looked like. The emotion of Bill’s character was so rooted in the eye, so having little things like that along the way allowed us to build it all together collaboratively, from the beginning of the shoot to the end of the movie.” Lame added that while the Cyclops scene was short in the final film, it was initially much longer. “We had so much interesting material, and we were constantly deciding between the puppet and Bill and what to use.”

De Jong also spoke about Troy. The colossal set spanned 2.5 acres, totaling over 110,000 square feet. The search for a location began in Turkey, but everything there “was so modern and contemporary and we just couldn’t find anything that would work for us.” After more scouting, De Jong found Aït Benhaddou in Morocco. “There were huge swaths of acreage, and I figured if I could build everything practically from the ground up and then you have the entire existing town, that gives us that set extension — but in real life.”

Looking back, De Jong reflected, “I don’t know how we did it, but it happened. It was a lot of moving parts and incredible artisans that powered through, and we got there.” She added, “That was one of five other countries where we were simultaneously building every single set.”

While the Cyclops scene was a puzzle, the beheading of Athena during the Sacking of Troy and the magnificent edit of the statue came together with ease, as it was already written into Nolan’s script. Lame said, “Chris is such an amazing writer in so many ways. He’s been doing this for so long, and he writes a lot of that stuff into the script. That cut was very important to him in the story because the connection between Athena (Zendaya), Matt, and what that all represents in Odysseus was such a huge part of the story and the reveal.” She added, “They shot that pretty quickly at the beginning of the movie, so we had that early on. Hoyte and Chris do such a beautiful job; it allows me to do my job so easily.”

As the conversation drew to a close, De Jong discussed the Trojan Horse. Each version of the horse stood approximately 35 feet tall. “The two things Chris was eager to get into were the horse and the Cyclops, and conceptually figuring out what we were doing,” De Jong said. Both needed to be practical builds. Staying true to the aesthetic, De Jong knew she wasn’t interested in the naïve-looking, hammered-wood type of aesthetic. Instead, she conceptualized that the horse would have been constructed using ship parts. “Conceptually, I was thinking they would have put this together with ship parts and shiplap. They were master craftsmen of their time.”

She continued, “I came up with this shiplap idea and they would have carved the head and the legs, but it needed to be large enough to have a belly where we could physically put the actors, the Imax camera, DP Hoyte Van Hoytema and Chris inside of it.” De Jong began building prototypes and models in Los Angeles with her construction coordinator Jonas Kirk. He came up with the idea of making a mold because they would need multiples of the horse.

In the scene where the horse is dragged along the beach of Troy toward the temple, De Jong said, “George Cottle (stunt coordinator) and his team got all 300 men that day; they physically tied ropes. There was no machinery moving the horse — it was the actors.”

article_text:
写真家・工藤司の個展「TSUKASA KUDO | so alone」が、2026年10月31日（土）から11月13日（金）まで、東京・代官山 蔦屋書店で開催される。発売後まもなく完売した写真集『ソーアローン so alone』のセカンドエディション刊行を記念する展覧会だ。

ファッションブランド「kudos」「soduk」のデザイナーとしても活動する工藤は、写真家としての制作に加え、2020年から出版事業「TSUKASAKUDO PUBLISHING」を主宰している。

本作の出発点となったのは、夏の終わり、小雨の降る朝に東京を離れ、海で初めて人物を撮影した経験だった。工藤は「ひとりは悲しいということではなく、ひとりで立っている。ということ」と綴り、自分と他者との間にある距離を「so alone」と名づけた。

今回刊行されるセカンドエディションは、モノクロームの写真で構成し、収録点数を増やした新版。表紙はポスターとしても使用できる仕様となっており、ブックデザインは初版に続き桂澤源が手がけた。

会場では、工藤自身が暗室で手焼きしたプリントを展示・販売するほか、写真集に関連するグッズも販売。10月31日（土）14～17時には本人によるブックサイニングも開催される。

タイトル

工藤司「TSUKASA KUDO | so alone」

場所

代官山 蔦屋書店 2号館1階 ギャラリースペース（東京都渋谷区猿楽町17-5）

会期

2026年10月31日（土）〜11月13日（金）

時間

9:00～22:00

料金

無料

Guide

10 Art Shows to See in Los Angeles This November

Yuntao Xu’s art show in a gas station, LA’s first gallery run for and by Black artists, iris yirei hu’s reliquaries for a dream, and April Bey’s alien tapestries of human life.

The art community in Los Angeles is digging deep into history this November, excavating and reframing it through novel juxtapositions and archival findings. Isabelle Frances McGuire tackles the Salem Witch Trials with a video game that bears uneasy relevance to our current age of creeping authoritarianism (just in time for next week’s midterms). Milano Chow draws on the archives of the LA Public Library to create ghostly architectural facades that seem at once familiar and foreign. At LACMA, an exhibition gives proper due to the city’s pioneering Brockman Gallery of 1967–90, which gave early support to scores of Black artists. And at the Brick, a retrospective brings together the two sides of Todd Gray’s long career: his commercial photos of musical acts and his post-modern tableaux, which themselves pull from archival images to construct new narratives.

Isabelle Frances McGuire: Joy is a Puppet

Bel Ami , 709 North Hill Street, Suite #105 and #103, Chinatown, Los Angeles Through November 28

Isabelle Frances McGuire plays with history, dusting off well-known figures and disrupting their iconic status to enhance their humanity. In Joy is a Puppet , she takes aim at the Salem Witch Trials, a dark period that has taken on increasing relevance as we slide deeper into fascism. The exhibition features a bronze statue, a trio of frogs, an assemblage of baskets, and an interactive video game in which the player takes on the role of a woman accused of witchcraft and must figure out their next move.

April Bey: All the Reasons We Never Tell Someone We Love Them...They’re Worthless

Vielmetter Los Angeles , 1700 South Santa Fe Avenue, #101, Downtown, Los Angeles October 31–December 19

Bahamian-American artist April Bey explores love, romance, and companionship in new fabric works on view at Vielmetter. These pieces represent the latest chapter in Bey’s Atlantica project, in which the artist assumes the identity of an extraterrestrial being and shares dispatches about human life with her home planet. Incorporating crushed velvet, metallic brocade, and sherpa fabric, the large-scale woven tapestries feature portraits that Bey took during a 2024 residency in the historically Black community of Orange Mound in Memphis, Tennessee, depicting scenes of queer intimacy within her opulent textile world.

Charles Arnoldi: String Theory

Michael Kohn Gallery , 1227 North Highland Avenue, Hollywood, Los Angeles Through December 19

Charles Arnoldi has been expanding the terrain of abstraction for almost six decades, from his early twig-and-stick constructions to his chainsaw-carved plywood works and hard-edge geometric paintings. String Theory presents paintings made between 2016 and 2019 in which networks of lyrical lines dance across the surface, their fluid energy contained by the rectilinear boundaries of the canvas. Balancing a sense of visual delight with formal complexity, these paintings are in dialogue with works by Brice Marden, Alexander Calder, and others, while branching out into compelling new directions.

iris yirei hu: Unconscious Relics

Official Welcome , 672 South La Fayette Park Place, Suite 46, Westlake, Los Angeles Through December 19

Iris yirei hu draws on dreams, ancestral knowledge, collective ritual, and elements of the natural world to ground contemporary issues within traditional frameworks. Unconscious Relics features new paintings, ceramics, and reliquary boxes adorned with images and objects that hold personal and cultural significance, originating from Tongva customs and Chinese herbal medicine. Juxtaposing these disparate symbols, hu layers various belief systems in order to create new mythologies for our current, troubled times.

Milano Chow: Fantasy Street and Deborah Turbeville: The Lifted Veil

Hollyhock House , 4800 Hollywood Boulevard, Barnsdall Art Park, Los Angeles Through December 20

Milano Chow creates stark, haunting architectural facades and interiors using graphite, ink, and photo transfer. For the works in Fantasy Street , she ventured into the archives of the Los Angeles Public Library, pulling images of early-20th-century movie theaters, shops, and apartments to construct fictional buildings through ink, pencil, and photo transfer. The works are displayed in an unfurnished room in Frank Lloyd Wright’s Hollyhock House and mounted on folding screens designed by Chow, putting them in conversation with the historic home and blending fiction and reality. Alongside this exhibition, Chow curated The Lifted Veil , featuring surreal, dreamlike photographs by Deborah Turbeville from the 1970s through the 1990s that resonate with her own entrancing alienation.

Yuntao Xu: Estranged Landscape

Adams Square Mini Park Gas Station , 1020 East Palmer Avenue, Glendale, California Through January 8, 2027

Estranged Landscape (2026) (image courtesy Glendale Library, Arts & Culture)

Los Angeles is full of art spaces in unconventional sites — strip malls, storefronts, apartments — and the Adams Square Mini Park Gas Station in Glendale fits right in with that tradition. Within this modest, window-lined box, architect and artist Yuntao Xu has created an installation inspired by the natural landscape surrounding the gas station that houses it. Composed of reflective fabric hung from the ceiling, fluffy textiles, and colored lights, Estranged Landscape echoes the forms of Southern California’s dramatic peaks and valleys with a campy, space-age spin.

Todd Gray: Church and State

The Brick , 518 North Western Avenue, East Hollywood, Los Angeles Through January 16, 2027

Todd Gray’s photographic assemblages mix images of art, architecture, and the natural world in ambitious tableaux that lay bare the intertwining threads of colonialism and culture. Gray got his start as a commercial photographer, however, when he was just a teenager, photographing bands including the Doors, the Rolling Stones, and Led Zeppelin; shooting album covers for Gladys Knight and Bobby Brown; and even becoming Michael Jackson’s personal photographer. Church and State brings together these two bodies of work for the first time, alongside biographical ephemera illustrating Gray’s personal experience as a Black man coming of age in Los Angeles during the 1960s, ’70s and ’80s.

Julie Tolentino: And Never Ends

Fulcrum Arts , 544 North Fair Oaks Avenue, Pasadena, California Through January 23, 2027

And Never Ends (2026) (photo courtesy Fulcrum Arts)

Julie Tolentino’s wide-ranging practice incorporates performance, sound, installation, scent, and text. Fittingly, her current exhibition at Fulcrum Arts aims to “decenter the visual,” encouraging visitors to utilize their other senses, especially hearing. Eschewing a static presentation, this new installation includes cultured crystals, an auditory composition, and a performance-based drawing, creating an environment that will continue to change and develop throughout the exhibition’s run.

The Brockman Gallery: Los Angeles, 1967–1990

Los Angeles County Museum of Art , 5905 Wilshire Boulevard, Mid-Wilshire, Los Angeles Through January 24, 2027

The Brockman Gallery was LA’s first major art gallery founded and run by and for Black artists, exhibiting the work of David Hammons, Ulysses Jenkins, Suzanne Jackson, Senga Nengudi, Betye Saar, and others early in their careers. Founded in 1967 by brothers Alonzo and Dale Brockman Davis shortly after the Watts Rebellion, the gallery served as a vital cultural and community hub in Leimert Park until its closing in 1990. This is the first large-scale exhibition dedicated to the gallery, tracing its history and legacy through over 60 artworks and archival material.

Reggie Burrows Hodges: A Theater of Dreams, A Theater of Miracles, A Theater of Passions

Art + Practice , 3401 West 43rd Place, Leimert Park, Los Angeles California African American Museum , 600 State Drive, Exposition Park, Los Angeles Getty Center , 1200 Getty Center Drive, Brentwood, Los Angeles Through February 28, 2027

This three-venue exhibition showcases the work of Los Angeles-born artist Reggie Burrows Hodges, with expressionistic paintings that highlight his deep engagement with art history intertwined with autobiographical narratives and scenes of contemporary Black life. A Theater of Miracles showcases the influence of Old Master paintings in his work, including several at the Getty, such as Jacopo Bassano’s “The Miracle of the Quails” (1554), which will be on display at CAAM. Meanwhile, A Theater of Passions exhibits new paintings inspired by the work of father-and-daughter painters Orazio and Artemisia Gentileschi in the Getty’s collection. Finally, A Theater of Dreams at Art + Practice reflects on the artist’s childhood growing up in Compton and his travels through Europe, where he encountered many of these Old Master paintings in person.

article_text:
Issue

New Currents: Heesoo Kwon

HEESOO KWON ,

Leymusoom Garden: New Sun , 2024, still from 3D animation: 14 min 21 sec. Courtesy the artist.

In Heesoo Kwon’s Leymusoom Sinmok (2023), thin branches gathered from Ohlone land are suspended in midair, bearing fraying, knotted strands of hanbok and sochang fabric, wool crochet, and other inherited textiles. These remnants of female labor are entangled with discarded hardware—LED lights, cables, a computer mouse—together embodying the digital mysticism that characterizes Leymusoom, Kwon’s autobiographical feminist religion-cum-artistic universe and the namesake of her fictional serpentine creator goddess.

Born in Seoul and currently based in the US, Kwon leverages technology and archival materials to create a “metaverse-sanctuary” dedicated to the feminine Other, subverting the patriarchal dynamics encoded in Korean folkloric belief and her own Catholic upbringing.

article_text:
Frida screenwriter and Selena writer/director Gregory Nava is mourning the loss of his friend Dolores Huerta, the civil rights icon who died today at age 96.

Nava and his wife Barbara Martinez Jitner were by Huerta’s side in her final moments.

“We were blessed to be by Dolores’s side last night in Bakersfield, to say goodbye and stand with her family in love. Dolores was a great light and a fearless warrior for justice. She set the world ablaze with her passion for equality and inspired generations to discover their own power,” they said in a joint statement.

Related Stories

Toho CEO Matsuoka Hiro On The Company's Decision To Self-Distribute 'Godzilla Minus One' In The U.S. -- Tokyo

Milwaukee Brewers Win First World Series In Franchise History

Throughout her life, Huerta fought for the rights of many, including, in large part, that of farmworkers and their families. Channeling that passion into action led her to co-found the labor union, the National Farm Workers Association, alongside Cesar Chavez, which later became United Farm Workers. She organized multiple boycotts that forced the agriculture industry to shift, leading to improved working conditions and the passing of legislation that secured the migrant farmworkers’ rights to bargain collectively, among many other achievements.

Watch on Deadline

Finding inspiration in Huerta’s life, Nava announced in 2024 that his next film would be a biopic on Huerta, a passion project he will direct from a screenplay he co-wrote with Martinez Jitner. Earlier today, Nava confirmed the script has been completed, and he and his team will be taking the next steps to move the project along.

For many years, Huerta turned down offers to have her story told on the big screen, but she changed her mind. In recent years, she realized that a movie would be a way to inspire the next generation of activists and organizers.

Nava and Martinez Jitner’s message also said, “In these last few years, Dolores and her beautiful family welcomed us even closer, entrusting us with the telling of her life-its extraordinary courage, its struggles and joys, its deepest pain. It has been one of the greatest privileges of our professional lives, and a deeply personal trust. We will honor it with tenderness and care, carrying her voice and her story to generations yet to come.”

The upcoming film’s producer Ivette Rodriguez remembered spending time with Huerta in the past three years as the legendary activist’s story continued to unfold.

“Dolores inspired generations to recognize their own power and fight for dignity and justice. This is an extraordinary loss, and my heart is with her family. It has been the greatest honor to know Dolores and to work with Gregory and Barbara, whom she entrusted with her life story. That trust is a profound responsibility—one that will be honored with the love, care, and respect she deserves,” Rodriguez said.

Huerta is also admired for being a staunch supporter of women’s and voters’ rights who didn’t shy away from pushing Washington to change policies for the better, even in later years. She is famously known for coining the term “Sí, se puede,” a rallying cry used first during a hunger strike in 1972. The term was translated into English as “Yes, we can,” most famously used by Barack Obama in 2004 during his run for the U.S. Senate and again in 2008 when he ran for president—both times with Huerta’s full support. President Obama awarded Huerta the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012.

Before Nava’s new film hits theaters, Huerta can next be seen participating in the Ellen Gavin-directed Blood Money , a four-minute short film that examines the billion-dollar business behind America’s ICE detention system, the human cost of immigration enforcement, and the power of collective action. The project serves as one of her last on-screen appearances.

article_text:
VENUS ALFA è un viaggio nel sottosopra della cultura visiva tra storie kinky, glitch culturali e cattive ragazze che sfidano gli stereotipi, hackerano il gender gap e amplificano il female empowerment.

In La morte ti fa bella (1992), Robert Zemeckis raccontava l’ossessione per la giovinezza eterna e l’estetizzazione del corpo femminile attraverso una commedia nera diventata cult. L’elisir dell’immortalità, agognato dalle protagoniste Madeline Ashton ( Meryl Streep ) e Helen Sharp ( Goldie Hawn ) e custodito dalla misteriosa Lisle Von Rhoman ( Isabella Rossellini ), finiva per ridurle a veri e propri manichini viventi, condannati a una manutenzione grottesca e disperata, mentre i loro corpi cadevano letteralmente a pezzi. Nel mondo dell’arte contemporanea, invece, il legame tra corpo, tempo che passa e mortalità abbandona i toni della finzione per tradursi in una ricerca espressiva lucida e spietata.

Se nel film la morte si manifesta come il paradossale prezzo da pagare per il tentativo di sfuggirle, nella storia dell’arte il rapporto con la mortalità si è spesso intrecciato alla figura dell’artista, al suo vissuto e alla sua stessa scomparsa. Per lungo tempo l’archetipo dell’artista tormentato, segnato da una vita complessa o da una fine prematura, è stato associato soprattutto a figure maschili, da Caravaggio a Van Gogh , fino a Jean-Michel Basquiat . Quando il trauma, la fragilità o la morte hanno riguardato le donne, lo sguardo esterno ha spesso tentato di ricondurre tutto a una dimensione più romantica o a un fatto di cronaca. Diverse artiste e studiose contemporanee hanno tuttavia proposto una prospettiva diversa, trasformando la vulnerabilità, la memoria e il corpo che si consuma fino a scomparire nella materia prima del proprio lavoro.

Un esempio emblematico è quello di Francesca Woodman , morta suicida a New York nel 1981 a soli ventidue anni. Spesso raccontata attraverso l’etichetta dell’artista maledetta, la sua fotografia rivela in realtà una ricerca delicata e rigorosa sul corpo. Nei suoi scatti in bianco e nero, la figura umana è sfocata, si confonde con le carte da parati che si scrostano o si fonde con gli intonaci di case abbandonate, esplorando con sensibilità il confine tra presenza e assenza.

Se con lei il percorso è poetico e intimo, la storia della critica d’arte Francesca Alinovi mostra un’altra sfaccettatura del rapporto tra vita, morte e racconto. Docente al DAMS e curatrice di grande intuito, Alinovi fu tra le prime a cogliere la potenza della Street Art newyorkese, portando in Italia autori come Keith Haring e Basquiat. Profondamente immersa nella scena punk e dark degli anni ’80, viveva l’avanguardia con un’energia e uno stile unici. Ma quando nel 1983 fu brutalmente assassinata nel suo appartamento di Bologna, l’attenzione morbosa dei media trasformò la sua fine in un caso di cronaca nera, feticizzandone l’immagine e mettendo a lungo in ombra la straordinaria portata del suo contributo intellettuale.

E come non citare la celebre “bad girl” Tracey Emin , da sempre abituata a mettere a nudo le proprie ferite, come nell’iconico My Bed . Oggi Emin sta vivendo una stagione di straordinario successo mondiale e consacrazione istituzionale. Dopo aver rischiato di morire nel 2020 a causa di un tumore aggressivo ed essere sopravvissuta a un devastante intervento salvavita, il sistema dell’arte e i media sembrano quasi volerla elevare a una sorta di martire contemporanea o figura salvifica. Emin, tuttavia, utilizza questo immenso palcoscenico per mostrare senza filtri i segni della malattia e i radicali cambiamenti del corpo, trasformando la consacrazione mediatica in una presenza potente, carne viva e priva di qualsiasi edulcorazione.

Dalla battaglia contro la Mietitrice al contatto diretto con lei, questa è l’inversione che fa invece l’artista messicana Teresa Margolles , portando l’esperienza vis-à-vis in galleria in modo crudo e sconvolgente. Avendo lavorato a lungo negli obitori di Città del Messico, Margolles, celebrata quest’autunno da una monumentale doppia mostra al MoMA e al MoMA PS1 di New York, utilizza nelle sue installazioni materiali reali legati al decesso e alla violenza, dall’acqua usata per lavare i cadaveri alla nebbia vaporizzata derivata da tessuti organici, trasformando la fine fisica in una traccia tangibile, poetica e al contempo spietata.

La morte ti fa bella, si sa, ma prima «Devi prenderti cura di te stessa. Ricordati: quando sei morta, sei morta!» (Helen Sharp, La morte ti fa bella , 1992).

article_text:
Chris Pratt is teasing his return to the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) to reprise his role as Star-Lord from Guardians of the Galaxy .

After Guardians Of The Galaxy Vol. 3 , the post-credits assured fans that the “Legendary Star-Lord Will Return,” but that has not happened yet.

With Avengers: Doomsday and Avengers: Secret Wars seeing the MCU come together, Pratt’s Star-Lord could potentially return in one of those films. In a new interview, the actor teased that something is in the works.

“I have a great relationship with Kevin [Feige] and Lou [D’Esposito], and there have been both ongoing conversations about how we make good on that promise and also hard action taken to make sure that we make good on that promise,” Pratt said on The Playlist podcast, The Bingeworthy .

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Michael Douglas Asked To Be Killed Off Marvel's 'Ant-Man': "They Wouldn't Let Me"

Mark Ruffalo Really Hasn't Forgiven Gavin Newsom For Backing Paramount-WBD Merger; That Could Be A 2028 Problem For Potential POTUS Contender

Pratt added, “So yeah, you’ll see Star-Lord again, which is very exciting, but I’m not at liberty to say when that’s going to be, but he’s not going anywhere.”

The Parks & Recreation alum first played the role of Peter Quill in 2014’s Guardians of the Galaxy . Pratt would then reprise the role multiple times across the MCU. In 2017, the actor starred in Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2, and in 2018 he reprised his Star-Lord role in Avengers: Infinity War .

Pratt would later reprise his role in 2019’s Avengers: Endgame , 2022’s Thor: Love and Thunder , 2022’s Disney special The Guardians of the Galaxy Holiday Special, and 2023’s Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 .

It was not only on television and in film that Pratt can be seen as Star-Lord, but he also appears daily at theme park attractions like Guardians of the Galaxy: Mission: Breakout! at Disney California Adventure and Guardians of the Galaxy: Cosmic Rewind at Epcot, the theme park at the Walt Disney World Resort in Florida.

article_text:
Films and events

Create

The Story of Documentary Film (The 1990s)

This fascinating chapter from Mark Cousins’ epic essay on the history of documentary chronicles a decade of formal reinvention and mainstream success.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Mark Cousins

UK 2026. 120min

Courtesy of Dogwoof

Language English

Introduction

Cousins, the creator of the groundbreaking The Story of Film: A New Generation and Women Make Film, trains his distinctive film-historian lens on the evolution of documentary. The result is a rich tapestry of landmark works and underappreciated gems. In this illuminating chapter, he guides us through the 1990s, a decade of filmmakers exploring bodies, spirituality, labour, war and politics, against the backdrop of rising commercial interest in the form.

Chloé Trayner

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury and nudity.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Act 3

The latest in Christine Molloy and Joe Lawlor’s series of cinematic essays is a rich and thought-provoking journey through ageing, legacy and the intersection between artistic and personal relationships.

Dependence

A filmmaker sifts through decades of home movies to understand her father, in this intimate study of what it means to love an addict.

Mark Cousins: The Story of Documentary Film

Acclaimed filmmaker and writer Mark Cousins joins us for a fascinating exploration of documentary cinema.

article_text:
Inspiration for a great storyline can come from anywhere — whether that be a classic work of literature or a great pop song.

It’s become somewhat of a bit for “Blue Film” writer-director Elliot Tuttle to reference Lana Del Rey’s music in his screenplays. He’d written three (as yet unproduced) screenplays before his feature debut about a fetish camboy who agrees to spend the night with an anonymous client, who turns out to be tied to his past. Each time, Del Rey released new music while he was working.

Related Stories

“She was always soundtracking what I was doing, so I would include one reference to her in every single thing I was writing,” Tuttle said amid a conversation Variety moderated in partnership with the Santa Fe International Film Festival to salute this year’s 10 Screenwriters to Watch.

For the climax of “Blue Film,” Tuttle borrows a line from Del Rey’s 2023 track “The Grants.” As the older man reflects on the memories he and the sex worker have made of each other, he says, “I’m gonna take mine of you with me.” (Del Rey dropped “There’s a Tunnel Under Ocean Boulevard,” which featured “The Grants,” while he wrote “Blue Film.”)

“It’s so funny because I really did not ever think that anyone would clock that. But then I also made a movie for gay guys, so I should have realized that someone would,” Tuttle quipped, making the theater full of film festival attendees laugh. Recently, he continued, a Del Rey fan account noticed the homage. “It was kind of the coolest I felt during the entirety of putting out this film!”

Tuttle wasn’t the only one influenced by pop music. While adapting John Steinbeck’s “East of Eden” into a Netflix limited series, Zoe Kazan found herself listening to a ton of Olivia Rodrigo, and she kept the Perfume Genius song “Jason” on repeat. “I listened to that probably hundreds of times, and it ruined our Spotify account for the year,” Kazan joked. “It like filled me with a sense of exquisite, precise rage, and that was what I needed for Cathy.”

When Aleshea Harris adapted her award-winning, genre-bending revenge play “Is God Is” for the big screen, she drew inspiration from works by Rihanna and Doechii.

“In my pitch deck for the movie, I had a still from Doechii’s ‘Crazy’ music video,” Harris said. “There’s a lot of unrepentant rage and self-embodiment in that video. And it’s a little weird, which I always thought ‘Is God Is’ is a few clicks left of center.”

Harris continued, “The summer I wrote the bulk of the play, I was listening to ‘Bitch Better Have My Money’ on repeat. … It’s very vivid. The video is so dope. There’s a revenge narrative inside of that video, so the muscle of that is certainly in the spirit of the film.”

When writing “Tony,” the untraditional origin story about Anthony Bourdain’s early years working in Provincetown before becoming the celebrity chef, writing duo Todd Bartels and Lou Howe only used his memoir “Kitchen Confidential” as a jumping-off point.

“My favorite part of the writing process is I see it as an excuse to go somewhere, and so we went to Provincetown … and spent the better part of three days hanging out in the greatest bar in America. It’s called the Colony Tap, which is a place that can only exist in Massachusetts. It’s sort of Celtics and Red Sox and maritime flotsam and jetsam, and sort of the bones of fishermen past,” Bartels said.

There’s something of an “osmosis,” he explained, about letting a location get into your bones like that. “Then when you have to go back to Los Angeles and you’re stuck alone in your cave with Final Draft, it sort of writes itself a little bit.”

When watching the finished film, Howe realized their early life experiences wormed their way into the screenplay, too. “My first job was washing dishes in a fish market on Nantucket. Todd worked in a fancy French restaurant when he was in high school,” Howe said. “There’s something about those experiences with working early in your life — you think you know how to do something, and then you learn the hard way that you really don’t — that feels very universal. That drew us into Bourdain, but it also made it feel so much more universal.

“Mouse” writer and co-director Kelly O’Sullivan summed up the experience of finding inspiration quite simply: “I feel like it can come from anywhere and everywhere.”

Take her film, for example: “Mouse” is a coming-of-age drama about a teen girl and her best friend’s mom who develop a unique bond after tragedy. “My partner and I were referencing ‘Psycho’ a lot, in that one of our lead characters dies very quickly, like 30 minutes in,’” she said. “We were like, ‘How do we get it to feel like this character, who is not our lead character, is Janet Leigh?’ Like we think this is going to be the star and then we subvert it.”

While crafting the film, O’Sullivan said she came to a realization about writing. “For a while, I thought it all had to be highbrow references, and then learning more about writers I love, you don’t have to just be citing poetry; you can be citing a TikTok account if that’s actually inspirational to you.”

“Sense and Sensibility” screenwriter Diana Reid concurred: “I feel like you’re always like swimming in this soup of influences,” she said.

For her adaptation of Jane Austen’s classic, Reid looked to Sally Rooney’s works and referenced another popular rom-com franchise. “There’s a big plot point in the film that’s based on ‘Bridget Jones’ Diary,’ which is kind of funny because it’s like ‘Bridget Jones’ was a modernization of ‘Pride and Prejudice,’ and then I took something from Bridget Jones to put it back in a very traditional adaptation of ‘Sense and Sensibility,’ so it’s like the snake is eating its tail,” Reid shared.

The panel took place the day before the movie, starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles, would open in theaters.

“I’m excited and nervous,” Reid said. “It’s such a privilege to work on — obviously — something like Jane Austen, which already has so much cultural capital and a lot of people care deeply about. It’s daunting, but then also it’s a privilege.”

Was anyone else anxious the night before their project debuted?

“The day my show premiered on Netflix, I projectile vomited, so I’d say I was really calm,” Kazan quipped, as the audience cracked up. “It’s great for me,” she added, smiling.

Indeed, things have really worked out for Kazan. “East of Eden” debuted at No. 1 on Netflix’s global chart with 6.5 million views and has spent 3 weeks in the top 10, tallying more than 25.3 million total views. The limited series has ranked in the top 10 in 80 countries and was the No. 1 series in 22 countries this week. (The limited series also drove a 156% global increase in first-time listeners to the audiobook of John Steinbeck’s classic on Spotify.)

“East of Eden” shared top spots on the Netflix charts with Felicia Pride’s series, the revival of the classic comedy “A Different World,” which debuted the week prior.

“I mean, the anxiety — I don’t even have words for it,” Pride said about waiting for her show to launch. “But I also felt like, ‘Thank God it’s finally going to come out.’ Like there was also a relief. You’ve been working so long … you just want it to come out after a while so that you know how people are going to respond and you can get over that part of the process.”

Pride needn’t have worried either. “A Different World” climbed to No. 1 in the U.S. (and at least 14 other countries), and has spent 3 weeks in Netflix’s global top 10, with more than 11.2 million total views. The HBCU-set series was swiftly picked up for Season 2; Pride took a break from writers room to fly into New Mexico to collect her trophy alongside the class of 2026, which also includes Beth de Araújo (writer-director of “Josephine”); Chuko Esiri (screenwriter and co-director of “Clarissa”); and Rebekah Taussig (screenwriter of “Being Heumann”), all honored in absentia.

Curious, Kazan asked how the experience prepping Season 2 differed from the first go-round.

“I just know what the show is now. I don’t feel the pressure of a season two,” Pride replied, sharing her sense of relief and newfound confidence. “I was very clear talking to my execs at Netflix, like ‘I’m just going to do the same thing.’ And there was support [for that], like, ‘Yes, let’s not reinvent this in season two,’ because sometimes shows try to do that, and I don’t think that is a great thing to do.”

Indeed, every writer has their own process — whether that means diving deep into the source material for an adaptation (Pride rewatching every episode of 1987’s “A Different World” while crafting the pilot) or finding deeper meaning in supplemental research (Kazan combing through Steinbeck’s journals); if it means holing up solo (like Harris did writing “Is God Is”) or trading pages with a collaborator (à la Bartels and Howe).

Watch the full video above as the panel unpacks their methods for getting their brilliant ideas onto the page, then the screen.

article_text:
Documentary NAZA , recently acquired by Neon mid-theatrical rollout , passed the $1 million mark this weekend. The Venice-premiering film, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor (two of the Oscar winning directors of No Other Land ) is eyeing $74.5k on 73 screens in week 4, for a cume of $1.07 million. Producer The Guardian had been self-distributing the explosive Israel-Gaza doc, which will continue to add more cities throughout October and November.

It’s a crowded specialty market. Neon ‘s Once Upon A Time In Harlem is eyeing an estimated $50.2k for its second weekend on three screens. That’s a $157.3k cume for the generation-spanning documentary. The distributor’s Cannes Palme d’Or-winning drama Fjord is at a $333k weekend (in week 3) for a cume of $694k.

Related Stories

'Clayface' Beams $43M WW Opening, Delivers Paramount-Warner Bros. Second No. 1 Weekend Win Since Merger - Global Box Office

'Clayface' Scares Off Elizabeth Holmes & Nathan Fielder From No. 1 With $24M; But 'You Can See Everything' Still Widely Seen With Near Epic $20M - Update

Other limited releases: La Bola Negra from Netflix had a limited expansion to nine theaters for a solid 3-day gross of $245k in week 2 for cume of $650k. Alamo Brooklyn was a top theater for the TIFF Audience Award-winner and these are solid numbers following a muscular debut last weekend. It’s the very first film the giant streamer is accompanying into theaters with official box office grosses.

Watch on Deadline

The Only Living Pickpocket in New York from Sony Pictures Classics, critically acclaimed and starring John Turturro, opened in 6 theaters to $156k. AMC Lincoln Square led with $33k, boosted by Q&As.

Mubi released Cannes Best Director-winner, Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland , at 4 theaters in New York and Los Angeles to an $83.8k opening weekend. Mubi noted strong audience demand with sold out shows across all four locations.

Moderate : Black Bear’s Wicker starring Olivia Coleman and Alexander Skarsgard is striking a chord with women, debuting to $5.75 million on $1,417 screens and a no. 5 spot.

Klara and the Sun (Sony) opened to $725k at 880 locations.

A Talent for Murder from Bleecker Street starring Helen Mirren as Patricia Highsmith debuted at 876 locations for a 3-day gross of $717.8k. Bleecker’s Alex Gibny’s doc Musk grossed $71k at 63 theaters for a $643k cume.

Jailer 2 from Shloka Entertainments hit $1.16 million in week 2 from 262 theaters for a cume of $7.2 million, as per Rentrak. By Nelson Dilipkumar. Stars Rajinikanth, Hrithik Roshan.

Wide : The fall indie crown continues to travel with A24’s You Can See Everything , at no. 2 this weekend in an expansion to 2,655 screens for an estimated gross of $19.5 million and cume of $45.1 million.

Fathom Entertainment’ presentation of Laika’s beautifully crafted stop-motion animation Wildwood followed at no. 3 on 2,779 screens with an $11.78 million debut.

Focus Features Sense and Sensibility , the latest adaptation of the beloved Jane Austen novel, on 2,572 screens in week 2, is at a $3.4 million weekend and a $16.7 million cume.
